result: The genetic ablation strategy using Tbx21Cre and Rosa26DTA mice successfully targets M/T cells. Tbx21::DTA mice survive to adulthood with reduced OB volume but preserved layer organization, and a small number of Tbr2+ cells remain after ablation.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the study as 'technically sound' with 'clear-cut' anatomical changes. The genetic ablation methods and characterization of the mouse models are accepted without critique, indicating reviewer support for these foundational claims.

result: Progressive M/T cell ablation in Tbx21::DTA mice shows that approximately 25% of M/T cells remain at P10, 3% at P21, and 1% at P120. Despite this drastic reduction, at P10 ~95% of remaining M/T cells had refined to a single apical dendrite innervating a single glomerulus, indicating normal refinement proceeds despite reduced M/T cell density.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'the initial pruning of the remaining M/T cell primary dendrite was unaffected' and describe this as a 'novel discovery.' One reviewer states the 'developmental refinement of apical M/T cell dendrites into individual glomeruli proceeds normally even when the majority of neighboring M/T cells are ablated.'

result: Adult M/T cell ablation (Tbx21::iDTR at P60 or P180) results in ~3% remaining M/T cells at P120. Strikingly, 36-48% of remaining M/T cells project apical dendrites to multiple glomeruli, with increased tuft length. This plasticity does not decrease with age, indicating that M/T cell density is required for maintenance of mature morphology.
evaluation: Reviewers describe this as 'the most striking result' showing 'the contrast between the normal dendritic pruning during early development and the expanded dendritic innervation in adulthood.' They note this is 'a novel discovery that can lead to further investigation of how the single-glomerulus dendritic innervation is maintained.'

result: When half the DT dose was used, 25% of M/T cells remained, yet ~40% still projected to multiple glomeruli. This suggests that multi-glomerular innervation does not simply occur because nearby glomeruli are empty.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without critique. The dose-response experiment is part of the 'solid support for the findings' noted by reviewers, contributing to the conclusion about M/T cell density requirements.

result: The ability of M/T cells to grow new dendrites and project to multiple glomeruli can be induced in adult (6-month-old) mice by reducing M/T cell density. Interestingly, only about half of surviving M/T cells show this plasticity, suggesting it may be restricted to specific M/T cell subtypes.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these observations as part of the 'clear-cut' results. The observation about heterogeneity in M/T cell responses is noted without challenge, though reviewers do not extensively discuss the subtype hypothesis.

result: Naris occlusion experiments show that sensory stimuli are not essential for the expansion of M/T apical dendrites into multiple glomeruli following M/T cell ablation. The percentage of M/T cells innervating multiple glomeruli was similar in closed (39%) versus open (44%) nares.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the authors conducted a few experiments to address potential mechanisms' and accept the naris occlusion data. This finding contributes to the mechanistic understanding without major critique.

result: Overexpression of Kir2.1 to silence M/T cell firing did not significantly affect the percentage of M/T cells innervating multiple glomeruli after ablation. This suggests the structural plasticity is not regulated by action potential firing in remaining cells, but may involve other mechanisms like increased synaptic excitation.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly states 'the evidence for the absence of a role of firing in regulating ectopic dendrites is still insufficient.' Another reviewer notes the mechanistic experiments are 'inconclusive.' The authors' conclusion about firing independence is questioned despite the data presented.

result: During development, OSN axons expressing the same receptor initially project to multiple glomeruli, then refine to single glomeruli by the first postnatal week. At P10 and P21, M72 axon targeting was normal in Tbx21::DTA mice, suggesting normal M/T cell density is not necessary for odor map formation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without critique. It is part of the overall conclusion that 'the normal density of M/T neurons is not required for developmental refinement' and is consistent with previous literature cited.

result: M72 axons projected to multiple glomeruli at P120 in both Tbx21::iDTR (adult ablation) and Tbx21::DTA (early postnatal ablation) mice, indicating that maintenance of the odor map depends on sufficient M/T cell density.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'OSN inputs to glomeruli lose projection specificity' after M/T cell ablation. This is described as part of the key finding that M/T cell density is 'required for maintaining specific connectivity in adults.'

result: Behavioral testing shows all Tbx21::DTA mice (early postnatal ablation) reached 80% accuracy in odor detection at 5% cineole and performed comparably to controls at 0.5%. In contrast, only 50% of Tbx21::iDTR mice (adult ablation) succeeded initially, with 21% permanently anosmic and 29% requiring training. This indicates preserved olfactory performance when circuits assemble with reduced M/T cells, but deficits when ablation occurs after normal assembly.
evaluation: Reviewers note 'it is interesting to see that the massive neuronal loss did not severely impact learned odor discrimination' and describe 'solid support for the findings, with a description of the structural and behavioral effects.' The behavioral resilience is accepted as demonstrating 'redundancy and robustness of the sensory system.'

result: Both Tbx21::DTA and Tbx21::iDTR mice could discriminate pure molecules and dissimilar binary mixtures (80/20) but had difficulty with similar mixtures (55/45). Tbx21::DTA mice failed to discriminate carvone enantiomers, while Tbx21::iDTR mice succeeded. This demonstrates remarkable resilience of the olfactory system despite reduced M/T cells and circuit disorganization.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these discrimination results as part of the overall finding that 'learned odor discrimination was largely intact.' The data support the conclusion about 'redundancy and robustness of the sensory system' noted by reviewers.

result: Innate behaviors were severely impaired: only 16.67% of Tbx21::DTA males mated (vs. 90.91% controls), and neither Tbx21::DTA nor Tbx21::iDTR mice initiated fights. AOB M/T cells were also drastically reduced (~1.5% and 16% remaining). This suggests AOB-dependent innate behaviors are less plastic and resilient than learned behaviors dependent on the main OB.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'mating and aggression were reduced' and accept this as part of the overall behavioral characterization. The contrast between learned and innate behaviors is accepted without challenge, supporting the authors' interpretation.

result: The refinement of M/T apical dendrites proceeds normally when M/T cells are killed soon after birth, but ablation after refinement induces surviving cells to expand dendrites into multiple glomeruli. This indicates that M/T cell density does not interfere with refinement completion but is essential for maintenance of apical dendrite stability as animals mature, with stability depending more on peer M/T cell density than other synaptic partners.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the authors conclude that the normal density of M/T neurons is not required for developmental refinement, but rather for maintaining specific connectivity in adults.' This core conclusion is described as well-supported, with reviewers noting 'the conclusions are now better supported by the data' after revision.

result: Odor map formation proceeds normally when M/T cells are progressively killed after birth, consistent with previous work showing initial OSN convergence does not require M/T cells. However, odor map maintenance requires a full complement of M/T cells—with reduced M/T density, OSN axons initially project to single glomeruli but eventually project to multiple glomeruli as animals mature. This demonstrates M/T cells are necessary for odor map maintenance but not formation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this distinction between formation and maintenance, noting that 'eliminating a large portion of the principal neurons in the mammalian olfactory bulb does not affect the initial establishment of the circuit but has an impact on its maintenance.' This is described as a key finding of the study.

result: Drastic reduction of M/T cell density (<5%) causes severe disruption of adult OB architecture with OSNs failing to converge and M/T dendrites innervating multiple glomeruli. Despite this, all Tbx21::DTA mice (early ablation) performed well on olfactory tests even with only 1% M/T cells remaining, while 25% of Tbx21::iDTR mice (adult ablation) became permanently anosmic. This suggests young mouse brains exhibit high resilience in learned olfactory behaviors, which may decrease with age.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the behavioral findings as demonstrating 'the redundancy and robustness of the sensory system' and note the study shows 'nearly normal odor discrimination in the absence of large portions of the olfactory bulb.' The age-dependent difference in resilience is accepted as part of the overall findings.

result: The full complement of M/T cells is not required for normal assembly of the olfactory circuit but is essential for its maintenance. Initial assembly processes (OSN targeting, M/T dendrite refinement) proceed normally despite >95% M/T cell reduction, but maintenance is perturbed with dendrite expansion and OSN misrouting. These changes can be triggered in adults after normal assembly. This highlights that in some brain regions, full cell density may be dispensable for circuit assembly but required for maintenance, and demonstrates remarkable reorganization ability of olfactory circuits preserving function after severe neuronal loss.
evaluation: This represents the main conclusion of the study. Reviewers describe it as 'valuable' and state 'there is solid support for the findings.' One reviewer notes 'the conclusions are now better supported by the data' after revision. The distinction between assembly and maintenance is the core contribution reviewers identify.
